topics.title: Numerical Concept 1: Indices and Standard Form
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: Give approximate answers to calculations. (u, s)
Write numbers to a given number of significant figures. (u, s)
Differentiate between significant figures and decimal places. (u, s)
State and apply the laws of indices in calculations. (k, u, s)
Use a calculator to find powers and roots. (k, u, s)

body.text: In an index form like 5^3, 5 is the base and 3 is the index (or power) — it means 5 x 5 x 5 = 125. The laws of indices let you combine powers of the same base without expanding them: multiplying adds the indices, dividing subtracts them, and raising a power to a power multiplies the indices.

body.latex: a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}, \qquad a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}, \qquad (a^m)^n = a^{mn}

body.text: Standard form (scientific notation) writes a number as A x 10^n, where 1 <= A < 10. The population of Uganda, about 45 000 000, is written 4.5 x 10^7 in standard form — count how many places the decimal point moves to get A between 1 and 10; that count is the power of 10.

Significant figures count all the meaningful digits in a number starting from the first non-zero digit, while decimal places count only digits after the decimal point. 0.00456 has 3 significant figures (4, 5, 6) but 5 decimal places. Rounding 3.14159 to 3 significant figures gives 3.14; rounding it to 3 decimal places gives 3.142.
